sermon:
## Strong and Courageous Over a Grave
*Joshua 1, the promise that outlives the man*

**Text:** Joshua 1 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 34:5-8 (Moses' death and burial) · Numbers 14:30 (the generation that would not enter) · Hebrews 11:1 (faith as assurance of things hoped for) · Matthew 28:20 ("I am with you always")

The book begins at a funeral. The greatest leader Israel had ever known is dead, buried by God Himself in a grave no man can find, and a whole nation is standing on the wrong side of a river with no idea how to cross it. That is where God speaks. Not over a victory. Over a grave.

**"Moses my servant is dead"**
The first words out of the LORD are blunt. "Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel" (Joshua 1:2). No eulogy. No pause to grieve the irreplaceable. God names the death and moves immediately to the promise, because the promise was never anchored to Moses. We are tempted to read the death as the end of something. God reads it as the beginning of something He swore to Abraham four hundred years before anyone named Moses was born. Deuteronomy tells us Moses died at a hundred and twenty, his eye undimmed and his vigor unabated, buried in the valley in the land of Moab by no human hand, and Israel wept thirty days on the plains (Deuteronomy 34:6-8). The mourning was right. A nation should weep when a faithful man dies. But the mourning could not be allowed to become a tomb the nation lived in. The servant dies. The promise does not.

This matters more than we admit, because we are a people who attach the work of God to the men who carry it. We say the church will not survive without the pastor. We say the ministry dies with its founder. We have stood at the gravesides of great men and quietly buried our hope with them. I have done it. I have looked at what a faithful man built over a lifetime and wondered, privately, whether God could keep it going without him. That is not reverence. That is unbelief wearing the clothes of grief. The God who buried Moses with His own hands was already speaking to the next man before the thirty days of weeping were finished. And the man He spoke to was not Moses' equal. Joshua had been the servant, the aide, the one who held the tent and carried the orders. God does not wait for another Moses to arise before He moves the promise forward. He takes the assistant and gives him the word, because the word was never carried by greatness in the first place.

**"Be strong and courageous"**
Three times in this chapter God commands the same thing. "Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go" (Joshua 1:9). It sounds like a slogan until you ask what produces the courage. It is not Joshua's temperament. It is not a pep talk. The courage is commanded because it is grounded in two things outside of Joshua entirely, the Book and the presence. "This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it" (Joshua 1:8). And before that, the staggering line: "Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you" (Joshua 1:5).

Notice what God does not say. He does not say the way will be easy. He does not say the giants are small or the walls are low. The previous generation died in the wilderness precisely because they measured the giants and not the promise, of all the men who came out of Egypt, only Caleb and Joshua would enter, because the rest let their fear become their theology (Numbers 14:30). God grounds Joshua's courage not in the absence of danger but in the presence of God in the middle of it. Courage is not the feeling that nothing can hurt you. It is the conviction that the One who swore the land cannot lie. This is what Hebrews would later call faith, "the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen" (Hebrews 11:1). Joshua cannot see the far bank dry. He cannot see the walls down. He is commanded to be courageous on the strength of a word and a presence, and nothing else.

**The presence that crosses every Jordan**
Here is where the grave at the start opens onto something larger than Canaan. The God who would not leave Joshua is the God who took on flesh and stood at the edge of a far darker river. Yeshua, the name Joshua carries, the name that means the LORD saves, walked into the flood of death itself so that the assurance given at the Jordan could be given to us at the grave. The same promise, made stronger, sealed in His own blood. "And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age" (Matthew 28:20). The promise still outlives the man. It outlived Moses. It outlived Joshua. It outlives every pastor you have buried and every leader you were sure the work could not survive. We are not the indispensable ones. He is.

So stop standing at the tomb. The God who buried Moses with His own hands is telling you to arise. Whatever you buried this year, a leader, a marriage, a version of your life you were certain you could not live without, the promise is on the far bank, and the same voice that spoke over a grave on the plains of Moab is speaking over yours. Be strong and courageous. Not because you are. Because He will not leave you.

The promise outlives the man.

## The Scarlet Cord in the Window
*Joshua 2, grace reaches the wrong house first*

**Text:** Joshua 2 · **Supporting:** Joshua 2:11 ("the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath") · Deuteronomy 4:39 (the confession Israel was given at Sinai) · Matthew 1:5 (Rahab in the line of the Messiah) · Hebrews 11:31 (Rahab justified by faith)

God sends two spies into Jericho, and the first person in the whole book to confess Him rightly is not a priest, not a soldier, not a son of Abraham. She is a Canaanite. She is a prostitute. And she says the thing Israel keeps forgetting.

**The confession in the wrong mouth**
Rahab hides the spies under the stalks of flax on her roof, lies to the king's men at her door, and then turns and preaches a sermon to two Israelite soldiers. "I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you" (Joshua 2:9). She has heard the reports, the Red Sea dried up before them, the two kings of the Amorites east of the Jordan utterly destroyed, and where her whole city responded with terror, she responded with faith. And then the line that should stop us cold: "for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath" (Joshua 2:11).

Read those words again and then go read Deuteronomy. Moses had said almost exactly this to Israel as the great confession of the covenant: "know therefore today, and lay it to your heart, that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:39). The confession Israel was handed at Sinai comes back out of the mouth of a pagan woman in a doomed city. She believes what the covenant people keep doubting. She has no Scripture, no tabernacle, no forty years of manna, no priesthood. She has rumors of the Red Sea and the report of two kings, and she stakes her whole life and her whole household on it.

That is the offense of grace, and we should let it offend us. We assume God starts with the respectable. We assume the gospel works from the inside out, that He saves the church people first and gets to the far country eventually. Rahab says no. Grace reaches the wrong house first. It walks past the religious and the credentialed and lands in the home of a woman whose name is a scandal, because grace was never a reward for the deserving. If it were, it would not be grace. The whole city had the same reports she did. The same evidence terrified them and saved her. The difference was not information. It was faith. And faith, here, is not a vague optimism. It is a confession about who God is and a decision to throw her household onto His mercy before the city falls. She does not wait to see whether the spies will keep their word. She acts on the report alone, the way Israel was being asked to act on the promise alone, and she does it better than they do.

**The cord that marks a household**
The spies make a covenant with her. "Behold, when we come into the land, you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down" (Joshua 2:18). When the city falls, every soul under that mark will live, but only those gathered inside. "If anyone goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood shall be on his own head" (Joshua 2:19). Her father, her mother, her brothers, all who gather in, spared, not by their worth, but by a cord and a promise. A whole household carried into the covenant on the faith of one woman and the mercy of a God who keeps His word to her.

We should not rush past the color of the cord. Scarlet in the window. A mark of blood-red that turns a house of judgment into a house of refuge, and a command that safety is only found inside, under the mark. The book does not draw the line explicitly, and I will not pretend it does. But the pattern is older than Jericho, a household passed over, spared by blood on the doorpost while judgment falls outside, the family told to stay in until morning. Rahab's window stands in the lineage of that doorpost, and both stand in the lineage of a cross.

**The outsider grafted into the line**
Here is what Israel could not have seen from inside Jericho's siege. Rahab does not merely survive. Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy, and there she is, named without apology among the mothers of the Messiah: "and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab" (Matthew 1:5). The Canaanite prostitute becomes a great-great-grandmother of King David and a mother in the line that runs to Bethlehem. The writer of Hebrews names her with the heroes of faith, alongside Abraham and Moses: "By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies" (Hebrews 11:31). The outsider is not just spared. She is grafted in. Her blood runs in the veins of Yeshua, the One who saves, the One who would receive sinners and tax collectors and the women no respectable rabbi would touch, because that is what He had always been doing, since a scarlet cord hung in a window in a city marked for destruction.

So who are you in this story? If you have been in the church your whole life and you have grown bored with the confession Rahab risked everything on, this woman is your rebuke. You have the Scripture she did not have and you doubt what she staked her life on. And if you are reading this from the wrong house, the doomed one, the one with a name you would not say out loud, then hear it: the cord is offered to you first. Not when you are clean. Now, while the city still stands.

Grace reaches the wrong house first.

## The Ark Goes In First
*Joshua 3:1, 4:24, crossing the Jordan on dry ground*

**Text:** Joshua 3:1, 4:24 · **Supporting:** Joshua 3:15 (the Jordan overflowing all its banks at harvest) · Exodus 14:21-22 (the Red Sea parted for the generation before) · Joshua 4:6-7 (the stones as a sign for the children) · 1 Corinthians 10:1-2 (the fathers passed through the sea)

There is a detail in this crossing that the text refuses to let us skip, and it changes everything. The Jordan was at flood stage. "Now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest" (Joshua 3:15). God did not pick the easy season. He waited until the water was highest, the river out of its banks and running hard, and then He sent the priests in.

**Into the flood, not after it**
The order is the whole sermon. "As soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water... the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan, and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off" (Joshua 3:15-16). The water did not part and then the priests walked through dry. The priests stepped into the flood first, carrying the ark, and the river stood only after their feet were wet.

This is the opposite of how we want God to work. We want the way cleared before we move. We want the evidence before the obedience. We want to see the dry ground and then step out. God hands Joshua a people who must put their feet in a flood on the strength of a word, and the parting comes after the step, not before it. A generation earlier, their fathers had walked through the Red Sea, and there the sea parted before they entered, the water a wall on their right hand and on their left, the dry ground appearing in front of them as they came (Exodus 14:21-22). They saw it open and then they walked. But that generation died in the wilderness in their unbelief. This generation is being taught a deeper lesson, that faith moves into the water on the word alone, before it sees. The same God, a harder obedience, because this generation will have to take a whole land the same way: stepping forward before the walls fall, marching before the city is taken, possessing on a promise they cannot yet see fulfilled.

**The ark goes in first, and stays**
Watch the ark. The priests carry it into the riverbed and "the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground, until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan" (Joshua 3:17). The presence of God goes in first and holds the ground in the middle of the flood until every last person is across. Not one Israelite crosses ahead of the ark. The presence leads, and the presence stays in the deepest, most dangerous part of the river until the work is finished and the last child is on the far bank.

We do not pioneer our own way and ask God to bless it after the fact. He goes in first. He holds the flood back from the middle of the river, standing in the place of greatest danger, and we cross on ground He is standing on. The dry path under Israel's feet existed only because the ark was planted in the riverbed. Take the ark out and the water comes back. The whole crossing depended on the presence staying in the middle. And the priests who carried it had to hold their nerve. Imagine standing in a dry riverbed with a wall of held-back floodwater on one side and a whole nation filing past, knowing that the only thing between you and the flood is the word of God and the box on your shoulders. They stood there until the last one crossed. That is what it looks like to trust the presence in the deepest part of the danger.

**The stones that preach to the unborn**
Then comes the strangest command. Twelve men take twelve stones from the very place the priests stood, and pile them on the far bank at Gilgal. Why? "When your children ask in time to come, What do those stones mean to you? then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD... So these stones shall be to the people of Israel a memorial forever" (Joshua 4:6-7). The miracle is turned into a sermon for children who were not there. God is already thinking about the people not yet born, building a monument so that a son three generations away will ask a question and a father will have to tell the story of the God who keeps His word.

We are not good at this. We cross our Jordans and we forget. We are delivered and we move on and our children grow up never hearing how their feet got to the far bank. We assume they will absorb the faith by proximity. They will not. So pile the stones. Tell the children what the water did when the priests stepped in. And tell them where this crossing points. Paul says the fathers "were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Corinthians 10:1-2). The waters that stood in a heap at the Jordan are pointing to a baptism, to a death walked through ahead of us, to a greater Joshua, Yeshua, who went into a deeper flood first, who stood in the middle of death itself and held the ground until His people could pass over on it, and who will not leave the middle of the river until every last one of His own is on the far bank.

The ark goes in first.

## Circumcised and Fed Before the Fight
*Joshua 5:1-12, consecration comes before conquest*

**Text:** Joshua 5:1-12 · **Supporting:** Joshua 5:9 ("the reproach of Egypt rolled away") · Genesis 17:10-11 (circumcision as the covenant sign given to Abraham) · Joshua 5:12 (the manna ceased) · Colossians 2:11 (the circumcision made without hands, by Christ)

The walls of Jericho are right there. The whole nation has crossed the river, the enemy kings have heard and their hearts have melted, and Israel is poised for the campaign of its life. And God stops everything to perform surgery on every fighting man in the camp. Before a single battle, He disarms His own army.

**The knife before the sword**
"At that time the LORD said to Joshua, Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time" (Joshua 5:2). The generation born in the forty years of wilderness wandering had never received the covenant sign. So on the edge of the conquest, with enemy kings watching from their walls and Jericho shut up tight, every man in Israel is laid up, sore and unable to fight, while God renews the mark He first gave to Abraham. "This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskins, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you" (Genesis 17:10-11).

The timing is deliberate and it is reckless by every military standard. You do not incapacitate your entire army in hostile territory in sight of the enemy. Unless the point is that the battle was never going to be won by the army. God will not let Israel into the land as a conquering force before they are a consecrated people. The sign comes before the sword. The belonging comes before the battle.

We have this exactly backwards in the church. We want to win first and worry about holiness later. We want the victory, and we will get consecrated once we have proven ourselves. We treat obedience as something we will arrive at after the success. God reverses it. He marks them as His before He gives them a single inch of ground, because the conquest is not how they earn the covenant. The covenant is why they get the conquest. The whole campaign rests on a people who belong to God before they fight, not because they fought. And there is a hard kindness in the timing. God does the painful, humbling thing first, while they are safe behind their own lines and the enemy is shut up in the city. He does not ask them to be holy after the adrenaline of battle. He cuts them, marks them, and waits while they heal, and only then does the war begin. Consecration is not the reward at the end of obedience. It is the door at the start of it.

**The reproach rolled away**
Then God names what has happened. "And the LORD said to Joshua, Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you. And so the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day" (Joshua 5:9). They had been slaves. They had been a people defined by Egypt, by what was done to them, by the shame of bondage, by four hundred years of someone else owning them, and then by forty years of wandering that announced their own failure to a watching world. God rolls it away. The place is named Gilgal, which sounds like the Hebrew word for rolling. He does not merely forgive the past. He removes its hold on their identity. They walk into Canaan no longer slaves, no longer the wilderness generation's shame, but a marked and renewed people whose old reproach has been taken off them like a weight.

This is the part I need most, and I suspect you do too. We carry our Egypt. We carry the shame of what we were, the reproach of the years we wasted, the bondage we cannot quite believe God would let us walk away from clean. And we try to fight our battles with that reproach still hanging on us, which is why we keep losing, half our strength is spent dragging the past. God rolls it away first. He will not send you into the land still chained to Egypt. He takes it off you at the border, names the place after the rolling, and then sends you in.

**The manna stops, the land feeds them**
Then the gentlest miracle in the whole book. "And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year" (Joshua 5:12). Forty years of bread appearing on the ground every morning, and now it stops, not because God withdraws His care, but because the promise has arrived. They eat from the land He swore to give. The provision changes form because the promise has come true. The wilderness food ends where the promised food begins.

Here is the line that runs from Gilgal to the cross. Paul writes that in Messiah "you were also circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ" (Colossians 2:11). The flint knife at Gilgal was always pointing past itself to a deeper cutting away, a consecration not of the flesh but of the heart, accomplished by Yeshua and not by us. He rolls away a reproach older and heavier than Egypt. He marks His people as His own before a single battle is fought, and He feeds them not with wilderness bread but with His own body. The order has never changed. He consecrates before He conquers.

So before you ask God for the victory, let Him do the surgery. Let Him roll away the Egypt you keep dragging. He always works this way.

Consecration comes before conquest.

## The Commander Who Takes No Side
*Joshua 5:13, 6:27, the walls of Jericho fall*

**Text:** Joshua 5:13, 6:27 · **Supporting:** Joshua 5:14 ("No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD") · Exodus 3:5 (the holy ground at the burning bush) · Hebrews 11:30 (the walls fell by faith) · 2 Corinthians 10:4 (the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh)

On the night before the greatest battle of his life, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword and asks the only question a general cares about. He gets an answer that overturns the whole way we think about whose side God is on.

**"Are you for us, or for our adversaries?"**
Joshua sees a man standing before him, sword drawn in his hand, and he walks up to him with the soldier's question: "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?" (Joshua 5:13). It is the natural question. On the eve of war, you want to know who is with you and who is against you. It is also the wrong question, and the answer dismantles it: "No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come" (Joshua 5:14). Not for you. Not for them. He has not come to take Joshua's side. He has come to take command.

And Joshua, who walked up like a general sizing up a stranger, falls on his face to the earth and worships, and the commander tells him, "Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy" (Joshua 5:15), the very words spoken to Moses out of the burning bush: "Take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground" (Exodus 3:5). This is no ordinary messenger. This is the same holy presence that met Moses, and Joshua's response is not a salute but his face in the dirt. The question of sides has been answered by being refused.

We spend our lives trying to recruit God to our side. We want Him for our cause, our nation, our tribe, our argument, our church. We pray as if the goal were to get God enlisted under our banner, fighting for our team. The commander outside Jericho dismantles the whole project with one word: No. He does not join armies. He commands them. The question is never whether God is on our side. The question is whether we are under His. Israel is about to win the most lopsided victory imaginable, and the chapter opens by making absolutely sure they know it is not because God signed up with them. He came to lead, not to enlist. And the moment Joshua understands that, his posture changes completely. He came with a sword and a question. He ends with his face in the dirt and his sandals off. That is the only right response to discovering that God has not joined your cause but is summoning you into His.

**A battle plan that is not a battle plan**
Then the strategy, which is no strategy at all. March around the city once a day for six days, the armed men in front, seven priests with trumpets, the ark behind, and the rear guard following, and not a word spoken. On the seventh day, march around it seven times, blow the trumpets, and shout. That is the entire military plan. No ram, no ladder, no siege engine, no assault. "By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days" (Hebrews 11:30).

God designs a victory in which Israel cannot possibly claim the credit. There is no tactical genius to point to, no heroic charge, nothing a soldier could carve onto a monument. Just obedient marching, silence held for six days, trumpets, and a shout, and the walls fall flat where they stand, and the people go up into the city, every man straight before him. The plan is engineered so that when the dust settles, no one in Israel can say their strength did this. The walls did not come down to a weapon. They came down to a word obeyed.

And the city is devoted to destruction, herem, given wholly to God, kept by no one for himself. "But all silver and gold, and every vessel of bronze and iron, are holy to the LORD; they shall go into the treasury of the LORD" (Joshua 6:19). The victory is not a prize Israel divides up among the soldiers. It belongs entirely to the LORD, which is exactly the point Achan will forget in the very next chapter, reaching into the spoil for himself, to the ruin of the whole camp.

**The weapons that are not ours**
This is where the book speaks straight into the church's chronic confusion about power. We keep trying to take our Jerichos by our strength, by cleverness, by political muscle, by the right strategy, by sheer force of personality, by whatever advantage we can manufacture. Paul says no: "For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds" (2 Corinthians 10:4). The walls did not fall to Israel's might because they were never going to. They fell to the LORD, so that His people would learn the lesson before they got drunk on victory and started crediting themselves.

And the commander with the drawn sword still stands at the center of it. He belongs to no army but His own. Yeshua does not come to bless our campaigns or sanctify our ambitions. He comes to command, and the strange mercy is that the victory He wins is one we could never have won, a stronghold no human strength could breach, brought down by His faithfulness and not ours. We do not fight our way into the inheritance. We fall on our faces before the commander, take off our sandals, and follow Him into a triumph that was never ours to claim.

The victory was never ours.

## The Sin Nobody Saw
*Joshua 7:1, 8:29, Achan in the camp*

**Text:** Joshua 7:1, 8:29 · **Supporting:** Joshua 7:1 ("the people of Israel broke faith") · Joshua 7:11 ("Israel has sinned") · Joshua 7:21 ("I coveted them and took them") · 1 Corinthians 5:6 ("a little leaven leavens the whole lump")

Jericho falls without Israel losing a single man. Then comes Ai, a town so small the scouts say two or three thousand men can take it easily, no need to weary the whole army. And Israel is routed. Thirty-six men die, and the hearts of the people melt and become as water. The God who flattened a fortress could not give His people a village. Something is wrong in the camp, and only one man knows what it is.

**One man, all Israel**
The text tells us at the very start what Joshua does not yet know. "But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan the son of Carmi... took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel" (Joshua 7:1). Read that sentence carefully. One man took. And the anger burned against the people. When Joshua tears his clothes and falls on his face before the ark and cries out asking why God has brought them across the Jordan only to destroy them, God's answer is brutal in its grammar: "Get up. Why have you fallen on your face? Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them; they have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen and lied and put them among their own belongings" (Joshua 7:10-11). Not Achan has sinned. Israel has sinned. They have stolen. The whole camp carries the guilt of what one man did in secret under his tent floor.

We do not believe this. We are individualists to the bone. We believe my sin is my private affair, sealed off in my own heart, costing no one but me, nobody's business but mine. The book of Joshua refuses that comfortable lie. The hidden thing one man buried in the ground lost a battle, killed thirty-six men, and put thirty-six families in mourning who never knew the cause. "I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you" (Joshua 7:12). Sin is never as private as the sinner thinks. It seeps. It spreads. It defeats people who do not even know it is there.

**The slow, deliberate exposure**
What happens next is almost unbearable to read. God does not simply point to the guilty man and end it. He has all Israel come near tribe by tribe, then the chosen tribe clan by clan, then the chosen clan family by family, then the chosen family man by man, a slow, dreadful narrowing while Achan stands there the whole time, knowing, and saying nothing. Tribe of Judah, taken. Clan of the Zerahites, taken. Household of Zabdi, taken. And Achan the son of Carmi was taken.

And only then, with the whole nation watching and the lot fallen on him, does Joshua plead with him: "My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me" (Joshua 7:19). And Achan confesses: "Truly I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and this is what I did: when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent, with the silver underneath" (Joshua 7:20-21). I saw. I coveted. I took. I hid. That is the entire anatomy of sin in four words, and it is the oldest sequence in the book, back in Eden the woman saw that the tree was good, desired it, took, and ate, and then hid from God among the trees. Achan only buried under his tent what every one of us buries under ours.

And notice the mercy hidden in the cruelty of that slow narrowing, he could have confessed at any point. Every step toward him, tribe to clan to family to man, was a step he could have stopped by speaking. He let it run all the way down to himself, gambling that the lot would not reach his tent. We do exactly the same. We wait, hoping the hidden thing stays hidden, hoping the narrowing stops before it gets to us, when the whole time God is walking down the rows toward us, giving us chance after chance to give Him glory before He has to drag the cloak out of the dirt Himself.

**The leaven and the greater devoted One**
Paul, writing to a church that thought one man's open sin was no one else's business, reaches for the same logic: "Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6-7). The camp is not a collection of sealed individuals. It is a body, and what one member buries, the whole body bleeds for. This is not ancient and irrelevant. This is your marriage, your church, your family. The thing you have hidden under the tent floor, the bitterness, the secret habit, the dishonesty no one has caught, is not costing only you. It is losing battles you have never connected to it. There are defeats in your life that have a buried cause.

Here is where the gospel breaks in, and it breaks in hard. Achan was devoted to destruction because he stole what was devoted to God; the herem he violated fell back on him and his household. And the staggering turn of the cross is this, there came One who was not guilty, who took the devoted-to-destruction upon Himself willingly, who became sin who knew no sin, so that the camp He stands in might live. Achan's hidden sin made all Israel guilty. Yeshua's open obedience makes all who are in Him clean. One man's theft defeated the whole camp. One Man's righteousness saves it.

So go dig up the floor of your tent before God has to walk down the rows to find it.

Hidden sin defeats the whole camp.

## The Long Obedience of Conquest
*Joshua 8:30, 12:24, the LORD fought for Israel*

**Text:** Joshua 8:30, 12:24 · **Supporting:** Joshua 8:34-35 (the whole law read aloud on Ebal and Gerizim) · Joshua 9:14 ("they did not ask counsel from the LORD") · Joshua 10:14 ("the LORD fought for Israel") · Hebrews 12:1 (running with endurance the race set before us)

This is the long middle of the book, the part we skip, chapter after chapter of kings defeated, cities burned, names we cannot pronounce, a closing list of thirty-one conquered kings read off like a ledger. But buried in this long grind of conquest are three moments that tell us how God's people actually live through the long obedience, and not one of them is glamorous.

**First, the law read aloud**
Before a single southern city falls, Joshua stops the whole campaign to do something that wins no territory. On Mount Ebal he builds an altar of uncut stones and offers sacrifices, and then "afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the Book of the Law. There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them" (Joshua 8:34-35). Half the nation stands on one mountain, half on the other, the ark and the priests in the valley between them, and the whole law is read into that valley, every word, with the women and the children and the foreigners standing there for all of it.

The conquest pauses for the Word. Before they take more land, they sit under the whole counsel of God, the blessing and the curse together. We want the curse left out. We want the parts that comfort and not the parts that warn. We curate God. Joshua reads all of it, leaves nothing out, because a people taking the land on a promise had better know the full terms of the covenant that gave it to them. The Word governs the war, not the other way around.

**Second, the covenant they should never have made**
Then the Gibeonites. They come dressed as travelers from a far country, worn-out sacks, cracked and mended wineskins, patched sandals, moldy crumbling bread, and they beg Israel for a treaty, claiming they have come from a great distance because of the fame of the LORD. And here is the line that indicts the whole episode: "So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD. And Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore to them" (Joshua 9:14-15).

They examined the evidence. They inspected the moldy bread with their own hands. They did everything reasonable, everything but the one thing, they did not ask God. They trusted their own eyes and their own judgment and walked straight into a deception. Three days later they learn the Gibeonites are neighbors, living right in the land. And then, this is the part that stuns me, once the oath is sworn in the name of the LORD, Israel keeps it. The whole congregation grumbles, the treaty is built entirely on a lie, and Joshua honors it anyway, making the Gibeonites woodcutters and water-carriers but sparing them, because the name of the LORD had been invoked over the oath. A covenant kept even when it costs, even when it was a mistake to make in the first place. We break our word the moment it becomes inconvenient. Israel, deceived and embarrassed, holds theirs, because their word carried God's name and that name could not be made a liar.

**Third, the conquest that was never theirs**
And through all of it, from the southern campaign to the northern, the refrain. Five Amorite kings come up against Gibeon, and because of the treaty Israel marches all night to defend the very people who tricked them. The LORD throws down great hailstones, killing more than the sword. The sun stands still over Gibeon. And the text tells us plainly why: "There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel" (Joshua 10:14). City after city, king after king falls, and the summary is never Joshua's brilliance: "And Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel" (Joshua 10:42). The whole long grind of conquest comes down to one actor. The LORD fought.

This is the part of obedience nobody preaches, because it is not a single dramatic crossing or a wall falling flat in a day. It is years of it. It is the long, unglamorous middle where you keep reading the Word in full, keep your word even when it costs you, and keep trusting that the One fighting for you is the one actually winning the battles you are too tired to win yourself. Hebrews calls it running "with endurance the race that is set before us" (Hebrews 12:1). Endurance, not a sprint. A conquest that takes years and a refrain you have to keep repeating to yourself when the names blur together: the LORD fought.

And here is the mercy hidden in the grind. The Gibeonites lied their way into the covenant and were kept inside it by a promise that outweighed their deception, a quiet foreshadow of every one of us who came in by no merit of our own, who came in by a kind of desperate ruse of need, and is held inside the covenant now by a faithfulness greater than our failure. The greater Joshua, Yeshua, fights the long war we cannot win, and keeps the covenant we could never keep, and secures the inheritance through every long year of it, so that the final ledger reads not what we conquered but what He did.

The LORD fought for Israel.

## Dividing Land Not Yet Taken
*Joshua 13:1, 19:51, the gift precedes the taking*

**Text:** Joshua 13:1, 19:51 · **Supporting:** Joshua 13:1 ("there remains yet very much land to possess") · Joshua 14:2 (the inheritance by lot, as the LORD commanded) · Joshua 18:3 ("How long will you put off going in?") · Ephesians 1:14 (the Spirit as the guarantee of our inheritance)

For seven chapters the book does the least dramatic thing imaginable. It draws property lines. Tribe by tribe, boundary by boundary, town by town, the land is parceled out by lot, the borders traced through valleys and along rivers and up to landmarks no one alive can find anymore. And the strangest part is what the text openly admits while it is doing it, much of this land has not yet been conquered. God is dividing up an inheritance Israel does not yet possess.

**The gift before the conquest is finished**
The section opens with an honest word from God to an old man. "Now Joshua was old and advanced in years, and the LORD said to him, You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess" (Joshua 13:1). The conquest is not finished. There is a great deal left to take, whole regions, the Philistine territory, the land of the Sidonians. And in the very next breath, God commands that this unconquered land be divided among the tribes as their inheritance. "Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and half the tribe of Manasseh" (Joshua 13:7). "Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses" (Joshua 14:2). The deed is handed over before the territory is cleared. The boundaries are fixed, the names recorded in the register, the lot cast before the LORD at Shiloh, for ground still held by the enemy.

The promise is so certain that God treats the not-yet-taken land as already theirs. This is how grace works, and it is offensive to the merit-driven heart. We assume the inheritance is the reward for the conquest. Take the land, then earn the deed. God does the reverse. The gift precedes the taking. The land is given by His sworn word, and what is left for Israel is to go in and possess what is already legally, covenantally theirs. They do not fight to acquire it from scratch. They fight to take hold of what has already been deeded to them by the word of God. The whole posture of the soldier changes when he knows the field is already his before he draws a sword for it. He is not gambling for a prize. He is claiming a possession. And the lot itself preaches the same thing. They do not divide the land by who fought hardest or who is strongest or who can seize the most. They cast lots before the LORD at Shiloh, so that the distribution rests on God's sovereign choice and not on human strength or merit. Even the way the gift is handed out refuses to let anyone earn it. The strong tribe and the weak tribe both receive what the lot assigns, because the inheritance was always about the Giver and never about the taker.

**The danger of an inheritance you never enter**
But the book will not let the gift become an excuse for sloth, and this is the warning we most need to hear. In the middle of the allotment Joshua turns on seven tribes who are sitting on their hands at Shiloh, content to camp at the edge. "So Joshua said to the people of Israel, How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?" (Joshua 18:3). There it is again, has given you. The land is already given, past tense, settled. And still they delay. They have the promise and they will not move on it. They have the deed in hand and they pitch their tents at the border, content to talk about the inheritance instead of walking into it.

This is the most common Christian failure I know, and I have lived it, and I have watched faithful people live it for decades. We have been given everything in Messiah, adoption as sons, the forgiveness of sins, an inheritance imperishable and undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for us, and we sit at the border. We treat the promises as theory, as doctrine to affirm rather than land to occupy. We can recite the deed in detail and we will not move into the territory. We know we are forgiven and we live as the condemned. We know we are sons and we live as orphans. Joshua's question is God's question to a church that owns far more than it occupies: how long will you put off going in?

**The down payment of a greater inheritance**
Paul takes this exact category and lifts it to its height. He says the Holy Spirit "is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory" (Ephesians 1:14). The word he uses is a legal and commercial term, a down payment, the first installment that secures and guarantees the whole. That is precisely what the allotment in Joshua is. The land divided before it is taken is the down payment of a kingdom not yet fully come, the first installment of a promise that guarantees the rest. Israel held the deed and lived in the partial possession, waiting to take the whole. We hold the Spirit Himself as the guarantee of an inheritance secured by Yeshua's faithfulness and not yet fully in our hands.

The inheritance was never earned. Not by Israel at the lot, not by us at the cross. It is given by the faithfulness of God, deeded before it is taken, guaranteed before it is fully possessed, sealed by the Spirit who is the first installment of glory. So stop standing at the border of what is already yours. Stop treating the deed as a wish. The land is given. The Spirit is the guarantee. Go in.

The gift precedes the taking.

## Give Me This Mountain
*Joshua 14:6, 15:19, Caleb at eighty-five*

**Text:** Joshua 14:6, 15:19 · **Supporting:** Joshua 14:8 ("I wholly followed the LORD my God") · Joshua 14:11 ("I am still as strong this day as I was then") · Numbers 14:24 ("my servant Caleb... has a different spirit") · Hebrews 6:12 (inheriting the promises through faith and patience)

Forty-five years earlier, twelve men went into Canaan to scout the land, and ten came back trembling about giants and walled cities, and the whole nation wept and wanted to go back to Egypt. Two men came back believing God. One of those two is now eighty-five years old, and while everyone else is asking for the easy valleys and the settled plains, he walks up to Joshua and asks for the one part of the land where the giants still live.

**The long memory of a faithful man**
Caleb stands before Joshua at Gilgal and rehearses the whole history with the precision of a man who has carried it for half a lifetime. "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God in Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me. I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him word again as it was in my heart. But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; yet I wholly followed the LORD my God" (Joshua 14:6-8). Three times in this short speech he returns to that phrase, I wholly followed the LORD. Not partly. Not when it was convenient. Not as long as the majority agreed with him. He stood alone with Joshua against ten frightened men and a whole weeping nation, and he held the line.

Back at Kadesh, God Himself had marked the difference. "But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land into which he went, and his descendants shall possess it" (Numbers 14:24). A different spirit. While ten men measured the giants and let their fear set the nation's course, Caleb measured the God who promised. And forty-five years later, having watched an entire generation die in the wilderness around him for the unbelief he refused to share, he is still standing on that same word.

We do not value this. We are impressed by the man who has a single dramatic moment of faith, the conversion story, the crisis met with courage. We are slow to honor the man who simply did not quit for forty-five years. Caleb's greatness is not one act of valor. It is the refusal to let go of a promise across half a lifetime in the desert, surrounded by the funerals of men who once outvoted him, never once concluding that God had forgotten what He swore.

**The old man who asks for the hard ground**
Then comes the request that should embarrass every one of us. At eighty-five, Caleb does not ask for retirement. He does not ask for the comfortable valley as a reward for long service rendered. "And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years... And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old. I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming. So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities" (Joshua 14:10-12).

Give me the mountain. Give me the part with the giants and the walled cities, the hill country that scared off ten men and a whole nation four decades ago. He is not asking for ease in his old age. He is asking for the very thing the nation was once too afraid to take. "It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said" (Joshua 14:12). This is a rebuke to the way we age in the faith. We expect the years to lower the stakes. We expect that decades of following God should buy us a soft landing, a quiet valley, a season of being served instead of serving, a right to step back from the giants. Caleb runs the opposite direction. The older he gets, the harder the assignment he wants, because his confidence was never in his own strength. It was in the LORD who said the land was his. And the chapter ends with him taking it, "And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak" (Joshua 15:14), the giants gone, the mountain his, his daughter given springs of water in the Negeb when she asked.

**The faith and patience that inherit**
Hebrews names the two things Caleb's whole life is made of: be "imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises" (Hebrews 6:12). Faith and patience. The faith to believe the giants are not the final word, and the patience to hold that belief across forty-five years of waiting while everything in him wanted to see it sooner. Most of us have one without the other. We have the faith for the bold prayer and not the patience for the long wait, or we have the patience of resignation without the faith that still expects. Caleb is the man who had both.

And here is where his mountain points beyond itself. Caleb could ask for the hard ground because the inheritance rested on God's faithfulness and not his own, "the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said." He wholly followed the LORD, yes. But a greater One followed the Father wholly, without a single failure, all the way to a hill outside Jerusalem, and secured for us an inheritance no giant can take and no death can break. We do not face our mountains alone or on our own strength. The same God who was with Caleb against the Anakim is with us, and the inheritance is sure not because we are strong but because Yeshua was faithful where we are weak.

So whatever the hard ground is that you have been avoiding for years, the conversation you keep postponing, the calling you talked yourself out of, the giant you decided long ago was simply too big for you, hear an eighty-five-year-old man who buried a whole generation of doubters and never stopped believing, and go ask for it.

Give me this mountain.

## Mercy Built Into the Map
*Joshua 20:1, 21:45, not one word has failed*

**Text:** Joshua 20:1, 21:45 · **Supporting:** Joshua 20:3 (the cities of refuge for the manslayer) · Numbers 35:25 (the manslayer returns at the death of the high priest) · Joshua 21:43-45 ("not one word of all the good promises... had failed") · Hebrews 6:18 (fleeing for refuge to lay hold of the hope set before us)

After all the conquest and all the boundary lines, God does something with the land that the empires of the world never do. He builds mercy into the geography. Before anything else gets settled, He sets aside cities where a man who has killed can run and live.

**Cities where mercy has an address**
The command is precise. "Appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses, that the manslayer who strikes any person without intent or unknowingly may flee there. They shall be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood" (Joshua 20:2-3). Six cities, Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron on one side of the Jordan, Bezer, Ramoth, Golan on the other, spread deliberately across the land so that no one is more than a day's hard run from safety. A man who kills accidentally, with no malice and no intent, a tragedy and not a murder, can flee to one of these cities, stand at the entrance of the gate, state his case in the hearing of the elders, and be taken in and protected from the avenger of blood until he can stand trial before the congregation.

Mercy is not left to chance or to the mood of an angry crowd or to how fast a grieving family can move. It is given an address. God plants it into the map so that grace has a location a desperate man can run toward. Think about what this says about the God doing the dividing. He has just spent many chapters giving Israel a land taken by conquest. And among the first things He does with it is carve out places where the guilty-but-not-malicious can be safe from vengeance. The same God who devoted Jericho to destruction builds shelters into the country for the one who killed and did not mean to. Justice and mercy, both written into the soil of the land.

And here is the detail that points forward: the manslayer must stay in the city of refuge until a specific event. "He shall remain in that city until he has stood before the congregation for judgment, until the death of him who is high priest at the time" (Numbers 35:25). His release is tied to a death, the death of the high priest, the one man who stands between the people and God. When that priest dies, the manslayer goes free, his guilt for the accidental blood lifted, free to return home.

**The tribe with no land of its own**
Then the Levites. Forty-eight towns scattered through every tribe's territory, because the Levites receive no single allotment of their own, the LORD is their inheritance. They are deliberately spread thin, planted in every region of the country, so that no part of Israel is ever far from the men who carry the Word and lead the worship. The priesthood is not concentrated in one capital where the powerful can capture it and the distant can never reach it. It is diffused into every corner, scattered like seed across the whole land, so the presence of God and the teaching of His law stay within reach of every tribe and every household. God refuses to let access to Himself become a privilege of geography.

**Not one word has failed**
And then comes one of the most important sentences in the entire Old Testament, dropped almost quietly at the end of all this boundary-drawing. "Thus the LORD gave to Israel all the land that he swore to give to their fathers. And they took possession of it, and they settled there... Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass" (Joshua 21:43-45). Not one word. Everything God swore to Abraham four hundred years before, everything He promised through Moses, everything He told Joshua at the grave on the plains of Moab, all of it, kept, fulfilled, settled. The land is given. The enemies are subdued. The promise is true down to the last word.

We live as though God's promises are merely probable. We hope they hold. We brace, quietly, for the possibility that this time He will not come through, that this time the word will fail. And the book of Joshua stands up at its close and says: count them. Go down the list. Not one word has failed. He is the God who keeps His word, and the proof is not an argument but a whole nation living in a land they did not earn and could not have taken on their own.

Here is where the cities of refuge come back, because they were always pointing forward. The writer of Hebrews describes us, the people of faith, as those "who have fled for refuge to hold fast to the hope set before us" (Hebrews 6:18), refuge language, manslayer language, the desperate run toward a safety we did not deserve. And remember how the manslayer went free: at the death of the high priest. We go free at the death of ours. Yeshua is the city of refuge with a name, the one we run to with the blood of our failures on our hands, and His death is the death of the great High Priest that sets the guilty free to go home. Mercy was built into the map at Hebron and Shechem and Kedesh. It was built into history at a cross. And the God who kept every word about the land has kept every word about that too.

Not one word has failed.

## The Altar That Looked Like War
*Joshua 22:1-34, build witnesses, not divisions*

**Text:** Joshua 22:1-34 · **Supporting:** Joshua 22:10 (the great altar built by the Jordan) · Joshua 22:24 ("in time to come your children might say...") · Joshua 22:34 ("it is a witness between us that the LORD is God") · Romans 14:13 (deciding never to put a stumbling block before a brother)

The war is over. The eastern tribes, Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, are finally going home across the Jordan after years of fighting alongside their brothers for land they themselves will never live on. Joshua blesses them and sends them off rich with spoil. And on the way out, at the very edge of the river, they build an altar so large it can be seen from a distance, and Israel nearly goes to war over it.

**The altar that looked like betrayal**
The text reports it plainly. "And when they came to the region of the Jordan that is in the land of Canaan, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh built there an altar by the Jordan, an altar of imposing size" (Joshua 22:10). When word reaches the western tribes, the reaction is immediate and total. "And when the people of Israel heard of it, the whole assembly of the people of Israel gathered at Shiloh to make war against them" (Joshua 22:12).

An altar outside the place God had appointed for sacrifice looked like the worst kind of rebellion, a rival shrine, a breaking away from the LORD, the very category of sin that had brought disaster before. And Israel had learned, expensively, at the cost of thirty-six men at Ai, that one part's sin defeats the whole camp. They remembered Achan. They remembered Peor. So they assemble the entire congregation for war against their own brothers, ready to spill the blood of the men they had just fought beside, over a structure they have not yet asked a single honest question about.

This is us, and we should feel the sting of it. We see a thing a brother has done, a choice, a structure, a decision that looks wrong from across the river, and we mobilize. We gather the assembly. We are ready to make war before we have asked one real question. The eastern tribes had bled for years to win the western tribes' inheritance, and the thanks they got, before a word was exchanged, was a nation arming itself on an assumption.

**The conversation before the sword**
But credit Israel for what they do before they strike, because it saves them from a catastrophe. They do not march first. They send Phinehas the priest and ten chiefs, one from each tribe, to ask. And the eastern tribes' answer changes everything. "No, but we did it from fear that in time to come your children might say to our children, What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel? For the LORD has made the Jordan a boundary between us and you, you people of Reuben and people of Gad. You have no portion in the LORD. So your children might make our children cease to worship the LORD" (Joshua 22:24-25).

The altar was not for sacrifice at all. It was a witness, a copy, a replica. They feared that one day, with a river between them, the western tribes would look across and tell the eastern children they had no share in the LORD, no part in Israel's God, that the Jordan marked them as outsiders. So they built a great replica of the altar of the LORD, not to offer a single sacrifice on it, but to stand on the boundary as a monument declaring that they too belong. "It is a witness between us that the LORD is God" (Joshua 22:34). The thing that looked like division was built precisely to prevent division. The structure that looked like war was an act of faith and fear that their children would be cut off.

How much of our warfare in the church is exactly this, a structure misread, a motive assumed, a brother tried and convicted in our minds before a single question is asked of him? The altar by the Jordan was an act of faith dressed in the clothes of rebellion, and only a conversation revealed the difference. We do not have those conversations. We assemble at Shiloh, we draw our conclusions, and we call it discernment when it is only assumption with a religious coat on. And notice who they sent, Phinehas, the man who had once driven a spear through open sin at Peor, the very man with the zeal to strike. They sent the one most likely to act, but they sent him to ask first. Even their zealot went with a question on his lips before a weapon in his hand. That restraint is what saved a nation from making war on its own brothers over a misread monument.

**The body that crosses every river**
Paul, writing to a church tearing itself apart over what looked like betrayal but was actually conscience and conviction, lands in the same place: "Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother" (Romans 14:13). The eastern tribes feared a river would one day be used to cut their children off from the people of God. The cross answers that fear permanently. In Yeshua there is no Jordan deep enough, no boundary fixed enough, to put one of His own outside the covenant. The outsider is grafted in, the distant tribe is held close, the dividing wall is torn down by the One who makes the two into one and reconciles them in a single body. The very thing the eastern tribes built an altar to guard against, He has made impossible.

So before you assemble for war against the brother whose altar looks like rebellion, cross the river and ask. Send the question before you send the army. Build witnesses to the God you share. Do not build divisions over a structure you never bothered to understand.

Build witnesses, not divisions.

## The God Who Keeps Every Promise, Including the Hard Ones
*Joshua 23:1-16, the faithful God also judges*

**Text:** Joshua 23:1-16 · **Supporting:** Joshua 23:8 ("cling to the LORD your God") · Joshua 23:14 ("not one thing has failed of all the good things") · Joshua 23:16 ("the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you") · Galatians 6:7 ("whatever one sows, that will he also reap")

Joshua is old now, near death, the wars long over and the land at rest, and he gathers the leaders of Israel, the elders, the heads, the judges, the officers, for a final charge. And he does something that ought to unsettle anyone who likes their God comfortable. He takes the great promise that the whole book has been celebrating, not one word has failed, and he turns it around to point in the other direction.

**Cling, and do not mix**
First, the command that holds the whole charge together. "Therefore, be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, turning aside from it neither to the right hand nor to the left, that you may not mix with these nations remaining among you or make mention of the names of their gods or swear by them or serve them or bow down to them" (Joshua 23:6-7). And then the heart of it, the positive command underneath all the warnings: "but you shall cling to the LORD your God just as you have done to this day" (Joshua 23:8).

Cling. The Hebrew word is the one used for a man holding fast to his wife, to be glued, to cleave, to refuse to let go. Joshua's deathbed concern is not that Israel will openly renounce the LORD and march off to serve Baal in a day. It is subtler and more dangerous than that. It is that they will mix. That they will keep the LORD and quietly add the gods of the nations around them. That allegiance will become divided so gradually that no one will notice the day it stopped being undivided. They will keep going to the tabernacle. They will also start mentioning the names of the other gods, then swearing by them, then bowing, one small accommodation at a time.

This is the particular danger the conquered land creates. The battles are mostly won. The crisis is past. There is rest on every side. And it is exactly in the comfort after the conquest that the clinging loosens. Israel was faithful when it was desperate, when the Jordan was at flood and the walls were standing and the giants were real. Joshua fears, rightly, that it will drift now that it is at ease. So do I, of every comfortable church and every comfortable believer, including the one writing this and the one reading it. We cling when we are afraid. We mix when we are safe. The greatest threat to undivided allegiance is not persecution. It is rest.

**The promise turned around**
Then Joshua takes the very sentence the book has been building toward and uses it as a warning. "And now I am about to go the way of all the earth, and you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed" (Joshua 23:14). We have heard this already, in chapter 21, as pure comfort and pure gift. But watch what Joshua does with it in the very next breath.

"But just as all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you have come to pass, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things, until he has destroyed you from off this good land that the LORD your God has given you" (Joshua 23:15). The same faithfulness that delivered every blessing will deliver every judgment. The God who cannot fail to keep His good word cannot fail to keep His warning. You cannot have the faithful God of the promises and refuse the faithful God of the consequences. It is the same faithfulness. It does not run in only one direction, blessing only and never judgment. The reliability that fulfilled every good thing is the very reliability that guarantees every evil thing if they turn.

We want a God whose reliability only ever works in our favor. We want every promise of blessing kept to the letter and every warning treated as a metaphor, a relic, a way of speaking the ancients used that we have outgrown. Joshua, on his deathbed, slams that door shut. The faithfulness is one thing, and it cuts both ways. "If you transgress the covenant of the LORD your God, which he commanded you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them, then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and you shall perish quickly from off the good land that he has given to you" (Joshua 23:16). The God who kept every word about giving the land will keep every word about losing it.

**The reaping and the One who bore it**
Paul says it without flinching, centuries later, to people just as eager to escape the principle: "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap" (Galatians 6:7). The same harvest principle Joshua names at Israel's border. And it is the hardest thing in the book to hold, because we would so much rather have a God who only ever blesses than a God who is true. But think it through. A God who would not keep His warnings could not be trusted to keep His promises either, because both rest on the same character. His judgment is the guarantee of His mercy. They run on the same faithfulness, and to want one without the other is to want a God who is not actually faithful at all.

And here is the only place this charge can finally rest. The covenant Joshua warns about, the one whose curses are exactly as certain as its blessings, was kept perfectly by no one in Israel, and the curses came, exactly as Joshua said they would, in the exile centuries later, the people torn from the good land just as he warned. But there came a faithful One who clung to the Father without mixing, who turned neither to the right hand nor to the left in the wilderness or the garden, who served no other god and bowed to no other name. And He took the kindled anger of the LORD upon Himself, the judgment we had earned, so that the warning, fully deserved by us, fell on Him instead. The faithful God who judges is the same faithful God who, in Yeshua, bore the judgment in our place.

The faithful God also judges.

## Choose This Day
*Joshua 24:1-33, choose the One who chose you*

**Text:** Joshua 24:1-33 · **Supporting:** Joshua 24:2 ("your fathers... served other gods") · Joshua 24:13 ("I gave you a land on which you had not labored") · Joshua 24:15 ("choose this day whom you will serve") · Ephesians 1:4 (chosen in him before the foundation of the world)

The book ends where it must, with a choice. Joshua gathers all the tribes of Israel to Shechem, the leaders presenting themselves before God, and before he presses them to decide anything, he does something that reframes the entire decision. He tells them the long story of grace before he ever asks for a response.

**Grace before the demand**
Joshua does not open with the command. He opens with God's own voice, speaking in the first person, rehearsing the whole history, and the history begins in an embarrassing place. "Long ago, your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates, Terah, the father of Abraham and of Nahor; and they served other gods. Then I took your father Abraham from beyond the River and led him through all the land of Canaan, and made his offspring many" (Joshua 24:2-3). Start there. Before Abraham was the father of the faithful, he was an idol-worshiper on the wrong side of a river, in a family that served other gods. The whole nation exists because God reached across that river, took a pagan, and pulled him out.

Then Joshua walks the story forward, Isaac, Jacob, the descent into Egypt, the plagues, the Red Sea, the wilderness, the kings east of the Jordan, the conquest, and nearly every line begins with the same word: I. I took. I gave. I sent. I brought you out. I delivered. I destroyed them before you. And then the verse that empties out every last claim to merit: "I gave you a land on which you had not labored, and cities that you had not built, and you dwell in them. You eat the fruit of vineyards and olive orchards that you did not plant" (Joshua 24:13). You did not earn one inch of this. Not the land, not the cities, not the vineyards heavy with fruit, not the olive trees old before you arrived. It was given. Every bit of it, given.

That is the ground of the choice, and the order matters more than almost anything else in the book. Joshua does not say: choose God so that He will be good to you. He says: God has already been good to you, has already chosen you, has already given you everything you have, now choose. The grace comes first. The demand grows out of the grace, as response to gift, not as bargain for favor. We get this backwards constantly. We make the Christian life a transaction in which our choosing earns God's blessing, our decision purchases His acceptance. Joshua stands the whole thing on its proper foundation: He chose first. He acted first. The vineyards were planted before we arrived.

**The choice that costs**
Only now, on that foundation, does the famous line come. "Now therefore fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD. And if it is evil in your eyes to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:14-15).

And when the people answer easily, quickly, almost glibly, "Far be it from us that we should forsake the LORD to serve other gods", Joshua does the strangest thing a leader has ever done at a moment of apparent revival. He tells them they cannot. "You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins" (Joshua 24:19). He refuses their cheap yes. He will not let them choose Him as though it costs nothing, as though they can keep the gods beyond the River in one hand and take the LORD with the other. He makes them count it. He makes them name the foreign gods they are still carrying, "put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the LORD" (Joshua 24:23), and swear the covenant knowing the full weight of what it will demand. A choice made lightly is no choice at all. He sets up a great stone under the oak by the sanctuary as a witness, because it has heard all the words, and a forgetful people will need a stone to testify against them.

We make our decisions for God the way Israel first did, quick, emotional, untested, the easy yes in the warm room with everyone watching. Joshua will not accept it. He drives them back to the cost, because the only allegiance worth anything is the one that has reckoned with what it will actually demand and chosen anyway. And the demand is undivided. You cannot keep the LORD and the gods beyond the River. The choice is exclusive or it is not a choice at all.

**Chosen before we ever chose**
Here is what Joshua could not yet see in full, though he was standing right on the edge of it. Our choosing is never the first move. Paul says God "chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). Before Abraham was taken from beyond the Euphrates, before the land was given, before a single Israelite at Shechem raised a hand to swear, the choice was God's. We choose Him because He first chose us. We love because He first loved us. The whole structure of Joshua 24, grace rehearsed at length, then choice demanded, is the gospel's own structure laid bare. He acts. We respond. And the response is real, costly, undivided, and it is still, always, only ever an answer to a love that moved first and reached across the river to take us when we were on the wrong side of it serving other gods.

The greater Joshua, Yeshua, stands at a greater Shechem and says the same thing in His own way, no one can serve two masters. He, too, refuses the cheap and easy yes; He, too, told the eager crowds to count the cost before they followed. And He, too, secures the very allegiance He demands, choosing us before the foundation of the world and holding us fast when our own choosing fails and falters, as Israel's surely would.

So choose. Put away the gods beyond the river. Name the cost honestly and take it. But choose knowing that your choice is not the first move in this story. It never was.

Choose the One who chose you.
